articles.title: When is Apple’s next event? Dates, rumors, and what to expect
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple has confirmed the date of its next event: this year’s September event will take place on Wednesday, September 9. It may not be Apple’s final event of 2026, however, with another launch potentially following in October.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple has confirmed the date of its next event: this year’s September event will take place on Wednesday, September 9. It may not be Apple’s final event of 2026, however, with another launch potentially following in October.

Apple typically has four main event windows each year: a spring event, WWDC in June, the iPhone event in September, and sometimes a further event in October. The company rarely confirms dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee it will hold an event in every window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next event will happen and what might be announced.

Fortunately, Apple’s annual schedule is fairly predictable, while reliable rumours often provide additional clues about what’s coming. That means we can make informed estimates about the timing of future keynotes and the products most likely to appear.

From the iPhone 18 lineup and new Apple Watches to potential Mac and iPad updates, here’s everything we know about Apple’s next event, along with the other events Apple could hold in 2026 and beyond.

When is Apple’s next event?

Wednesday September 9, 2026

Apple announced the date of it’s September event on August 26, two weeks before the event is scheduled to be held on September 9.

Based on Apple’s typical event schedule, we had already predicted that the annual iPhone launch would take place on this date. September 9 was the most likely date because September 7 is labor day and Apple would not usually hold an event the day after a public holiday.

Earlier in August the company asked Apple Store staff to apply for an “ Event Support Experience Program ” to enter a lottery for the opportunity to assist with an Apple event scheduled for the first half of September.

As in previous years, Apple is expected to livestream the event, allowing viewers around the world to watch the company unveil its latest products. One notable change this year is that the keynote is expected to be hosted by John Ternus, who is set to succeed Tim Cook as Apple’s CEO following Cook’s retirement.

Apple event calendar 2026

Apple has held two events so far in 2026, although the first was not an event in the traditional sense. On March 4, the company invited select media to hands-on “experiences” in multiple locations. In the run-up to that date, Apple also launched several products via press release, including the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, and MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max, M5 MacBook Air and the MacBook Neo.

The second event was WWDC, which began with a keynote on June 8. At the WWDC keynote Apple outlined the upcoming changes to its operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Looking ahead to the fall, Apple is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, a foldable iPhone Ultra, and more at an Apple event on September 9.

A second, late-fall event in October or November is possible, though less certain and typically focused on Macs or iPads.

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: I've played Heroes of Might and Magic 3: Remake, and I still can't believe we're getting 2 HoMMs in the same year
articles.subtitle: Ubisoft is going all in on fantasy tactics.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
After lying fallow for over a decade, Heroes of Might and Magic is enjoying a bit of a renaissance. Earlier this year, Heroes of Might and Magic: Olden Era launched into early access and will hit 1.0 in 2027. And now it's going to be joined by an old friend with a new look. The series' golden child, Heroes of Might and Magic 3, is back. Again.

HoMM 3 Remake is actually the third version of the third game in the series, which was remastered back in 2015. At a glance, however, you could be forgiven for assuming that it's a brand new entry, as it boasts a new art style along with a few more tweaks. But this is still absolutely HoMM 3.

I took it for a spin over a couple of hours ahead of its Gamescom reveal, playing the simple campaign prologue and the Arrogance scenario—a popular map first introduced in HoMM 3: The Shadow of Death. It's a compact, well-paced adventure that I remember being a good place to start when you wanted to delve into multiplayer (or if you just wanted a fun comp stomp).

This remains true in the remake. It's a four-player deal, and each starting position is close to a second town of the same faction, rapidly expanding your ability to recruit big unit stacks and making it easier to support multiple heroes early on. With entrances to the underworld close by, and nearby shipyards letting you cross the tiny ocean, it gives you the full HoMM 3 experience extremely quickly.

I confess, however, that I did embarrass myself a little bit. It's been a while since I've played HoMM 3, but I've been playing Olden Era in early access, so I expected to crush the AI. Unfortunately, I spent too much time just mucking around and fiddling with my army composition, so by the end I'd been outpaced by my computer opponents. I'm still convinced I could have clawed my way back, but we'll never know.

So this is largely the game you'll remember, but with some convenient quality-of-life improvements. Of particular note is the ability to see movement ranges for enemy troops, letting you identify which of your units might be at risk on the enemy turn—something that exists in the later HoMMs, but not HoMM 3 or its 2015 HD remaster.

If you don't remember because you never played the original, here's the skinny: you command heroes and their armies as they scoot off on grand adventures, hassling monsters, conquering towns and gobbling up resources. Inside those conquered towns, you can construct a plethora of buildings—most of which can be upgraded—allowing you to recruit more units and heroes, as well as unlocking new spells.

Each day lets your heroes travel a specific distance, and as time moves inexorably forward, your recruitment pool and treasury will expand, allowing you to field larger armies and more heroes. You'll eventually have hordes of dragons, giants, angels and demons ready to smite your foes in grid-based battles.

The hallmark of the series—and 3 in particular—is how easy it is to get to grips with, which belies its impressive depth. There's an accessible lightness to the proceedings, accentuated by a frequently whimsical tone, that eases you into a level of complexity that would otherwise be daunting. There are so many layers to juggle—economic management, big-picture strategy, tactical combat, RPG systems, and then the literal layers, as you try to conquer both the overground and underground regions.

HoMM 3 was exceptional in 1999, and age has not tarnished it.

The most obvious change in the remake is the art style, and this is something I'm a bit more ambivalent about. It's vividly colourful, fantastical fare, with units that are considerably more detailed than its predecessor's. The combat animations are cracking, too, making each attack more dramatic and weighty. The quality is there, then, but I fear the soul might be lacking.

OG HoMM 3 simply had a bit more character, with big, bold monster designs. It veered towards the cartoonish, certainly, but these goofy-looking units had a lot of rizz. The remake may have smoothed out the edges too much, aiming for fidelity over personality. And this is more obvious because we have another modern HoMM with which we can compare it.

HoMM: Olden Era's mere existence makes this remake pretty unusual. Olden Era is a completely new entry in the series, but it's obviously a spiritual successor to HoMM 3, both mechanically and aesthetically. It feels like a natural evolution. So it does feel bizarre to see it now sharing the limelight with a remake. There's just a heck of a lot of overlap.

Still, after waiting over a decade for more HoMM, I'm not going to turn my nose up at two coming along at the same time. HoMM 3 Remake launches next year, and Olden Era should be leaving early access then, so tactics nerds will have plenty to keep them occupied.

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered: Everything new coming in the big free upgrade
articles.subtitle: Get psyched for armor transmogs, folks.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
After 11 years, The Witcher 3 is getting a new story expansion and a remaster. CD Projekt Red has announced The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered, which is coming in 2026 and will be a free upgrade for all current owners of the game, paving the way for the shiny new DLC coming next year. It isn't just a technical update, either: CDPR is making changes to The Witcher 3's combat, skill system, and hey, transmogs!

Witcher 3 Remastered release date

The Witcher 3 Remastered release date

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered launches on September 29, 2026. That's only a month away from the day it was announced, which is a treat! It was revealed just before the teaser trailer for the new expansion Songs of the Past, but that's not coming until 2027.

The remaster is a free update and the original DLCs are now free

The Witcher 3 Remastered will replace the current "Complete Edition" on storefronts when it launches in September. It will also be a free upgrade for anyone who already owns the base game The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. The original two story expansions Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine have also been made free for all base game owners in an update the same day as the remaster announcement.

There's a good chance you do already have those expansions either from the Game of the Year edition years back or the more recent Complete Edition that's been the default version for sale since 2022. If not though, they're yours now!

Witcher 3 Remastered features

Here's what CDPR told PC Gamer about the remaster

Our own Josh Wolens got to see The Witcher 3 Remastered (and the Songs of the Past expansion ) played at Gamescom in August and talked with CDPR about the upgrades a bit.

CDPR's executive producer of external projects Jakub Kutrzuba told Josh that it wanted to think about what The Witcher 3 would play like if it were launching in 2026.

"We put a lot of our time into how the game actually plays," says Kutrzuba. "So, the animation system, the camera work, small quality of life improvements, accessibility changes, enemy behaviour in combat, maybe the pathfinding for the roads, etcetera—these are areas of the game which we know could cause some frustration here and there.

"We went through all of them and asked ourselves, 'What can we do about it, without rebuilding the game from scratch?' And we have changed a lot… the game just plays smoother, you know? There's no immersion-breakers anymore, I would say."

What's new in the remaster?

You can check whether this update has been installed by opening System Information via About This Mac, and selecting the Installations item under Software.

Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

The Mac mini boasts fast processors, and rivals even Apple’s most pro computers despite costing significantly less. However, as great as it is, there is a problem with the Mac mini—the at-purchase storage upgrades are pricey and after you buy one, it’s nearly impossible to upgrade its internal components. However, we’re here to help.

There are two basic Mac mini models: the latest M4/M5/M6 mini (5 inches square, 2 inches deep) and older M1/M2 mini (7.7 inches square, 1.4 inches deep). Here, we have rounded up the best hardware upgrades and accessories you can buy for either the old or newer models. Most of the M1/M2 tips work with the Apple Studio, too, as that remains the same size.

Apple doesn’t let you upgrade the Mac mini with inexpensive third-party components such as RAM or internal storage, and it prices its custom-build options at the very high end of affordability. With the earlier Mac mini Apple fixed the RAM to the processor and the SSD to the logic board so they couldn’t be swapped out after you buy one. The M4/M5/M6 mini is different with a detachable SSD but swapping this out is beyond most mere mortals.

Here we look at your best Mac mini upgrade options, adding: storage, memory, screen, speakers and microphone. If you want to jump straight to the reviews:

Hubs and docks for new Mac mini

Hubs and docks for Mac mini M2

Other Mac mini accessories

Upgrading the Mac mini: Adding memory and storage

In our FAQ at the foot of this feature we go into more detail about the difficulties of upgrading the Mac mini’s internal components—as it is with most Macs. There are solutions that are quite messy, such as adding external storage.

Foundry

Adding external storage

The simplest way to add storage to a Mac mini is the same as any other Mac: Connect an external hard drive or SSD using one of the Thunderbolt ports on the back of the computer. Even the slowest Solid-state drives (SSD) are faster than mechanical hard disk drives (HDD), but look out for speed differences—entry-level SSDs provide speeds of around 500MBps, while more advanced models can step up to 2,000MBps or even 6,000MBps. See SSD or HDD in the FAQs.

Another way to add inexpensive portable storage is via an SD or microSD card—once the go-to storage format for camera users but also a great format for cheap and portable backup and archive storage. Sadly, the Mac mini doesn’t have a card reader slot, so you’ll need to add one, such as this UGreen USB-C SD Card Reader for $15.

But these are admittedly ugly methods. You’ll have wires hanging out of the back of your Mac mini and a desk cluttered with drives. It’s neater to keep storage hidden inside. Apple won’t let you do it, but there are some great solutions that we have tested here.

Adding Internal storage

The best option is to get more internal storage in your Mac mini, but Apple’s custom-built pricing means upgrading a 256GB model to 1TB will cost you an extra $500, and 2TB will cost $1,000, while M5 Pro options cost even more: 4TB is $1,800 and 8TB will set you back a whopping $3,800.

If you can’t swing the prices for more storage or just decide later that you need more, there are hardware solutions that connect to the mini without messing up the footprint of the small computer. We’ve tested and reviewed these Mac mini storage accessories for you. The tested Mac mini hubs feature upgradeable and inexpensive internal storage plus a range of extra ports, supporting the NVMe form factors that resemble a stick of chewing gum.

Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages.

OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings.

Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks and how to revoke access.

It also lists a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts: “If your task is set to Full access or otherwise disables approval prompts, Apple Messages may be unable to show the confirmation needed to send. Switch to Ask for approval or Approve for me and try again.”

How OpenAI’s Messages plugin works on the Mac

OpenAI explains that the optional Messages plugin runs locally on the Mac. Like other ChatGPT/Codex features including Computer Use, it relies on macOS system technologies like AppleScript and Accessibility.

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

And unlike Siri AI, it doesn’t rely on an index of content from Messages. ChatGPT for Mac only uses the data when directed and with permission.

As you can see below, once enabled by the user, ChatGPT is super clear in what it does with messages, especially sending on your behalf when asked.

For these reasons, it shouldn’t be a privacy concern for Apple. The data exists as files on your Mac, and you need to give ChatGPT permission to work with the files. OpenAI also isn’t the only AI company to develop similar tools. It’s just a benefit of the Mac being a more capable operating system than mobile platforms.

articles.title: Blue Dragon has been stuck on the Xbox 360 for 20 years, but no longer: a fantastic unofficial PC port unlocks the FPS, goes 4K, and even adds mod support
articles.subtitle: This Xbox 360 recompilation proves how good fan ports can be when they aren't vibe-coded.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
When Final Fantasy creator Hironobu Sakaguchi left Square Enix in the early 2000s, he started a new studio, Mistwalker, to keep making RPGs. For the last 20 years, every single one of his games with the exception of Fantasian has been stuck on one defunct console or another, never ported or re-released. And that's a shame, because some of them are great RPGs.

Or I should say it was a shame, until now—because as of Friday, Blue Dragon will be playable on PC thanks to a fan-made port that's likely far more impressive than an official release ever would've been.

re:Blue, a static recompilation of the Dragon Quest-inspired JRPG, follows in the footsteps of the unofficial Sonic Unleashed PC port that proved how effective fan-made ports can be. These projects cleverly translate the original game code to run natively on modern PCs, but don't include any of the original assets to avoid copyright issues.

This technique has proven so popular that it's inspired a wave of AI vibe-coded ports that don't take the time and care to thoroughly adapt the original game to PC. But in spite of that, the good projects—like the recent Zelda: Twilight Princess port —have made it one of the most exciting things happening in games right now.

"My standards have always been pretty high when it comes to this kind of stuff—I like to make quality products," says Tom, the programmer behind re:Blue as well as ReXGlue, a toolset meant to help developers create more recompilations of Xbox 360 games like Blue Dragon. Tom introduced ReXGlue earlier this year, but has spent much of 2026 working on his port of Blue Dragon as a showcase for what his tools are capable of.

Some other ports have beaten Tom to the punch by quickly releasing rough works in progress, but re:Blue is by far the most polished and fully featured recompilation built using ReXGlue.

And the game deserves it: while it looks very much like Dragon Quest thanks to Akira Toriyama's art, there are some fun RPG class system ideas and turn order jostling hiding within what at first appears to be a rudimentary turn-based system.

More importantly for Tom, he's got backup from several superfans helping develop the port, and it presented a juicy technical challenge: a three-DVD game built on an engine that has never been documented.

I've been playing early builds over the last month, and have been surprised by how much better it looks and runs on my PC than many Japanese PC games did in the 2000s.

Aspect ratios 16:9, 4:3, 16:10, 21:9, 32:9, plus auto and stretch

Four quality presets, Low through Ultra

MSAA up to 8x or SSAA up to 4x

articles.title: Mac-ify your iPad with these 10 must-have accessories
articles.subtitle: Macworld Every year, iPadOS borrows a couple of desktop features, bringing Apple’s tablet closer to the Mac. At this point, some professionals have effectively replaced their MacBooks with iPads, simplifying their setups and making them more portable.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Every year, iPadOS borrows a couple of desktop features, bringing Apple’s tablet closer to the Mac. At this point, some professionals have effectively replaced their MacBooks with iPads, simplifying their setups and making them more portable. An iPad on its own, however, is insufficient to mimic a MacBook.

One cannot practically type long-form text using the virtual keyboard or rely exclusively on touch controls for daily tasks. Fortunately, with just a few accessories, you can completely transform your iPad experience and upgrade it to a MacBook-like computer.

Keyboard

A keyboard is the most essential productivity accessory you can get for your iPad. Not only does it make typing more intuitive, but it also unlocks advanced keyboard shortcuts across apps—accelerating your workflows in the process. Luckily, iPadOS supports a wide range of keyboards, including most standard Bluetooth ones.

Apple sells the Magic Keyboard for various iPad models, which doubles as a stand and protective case. It also includes an embedded trackpad, essentially turning your iPad into a laptop. For something more budget-friendly, you can’t go wrong with the Logitech Keys-to-Go Bluetooth Keyboard. It is designed specifically for Apple products, supports multi-device connections, and features a portable design.

Foundry

Mouse

Like keyboards, iPadOS supports most Bluetooth mice and trackpads, and will show a dedicated cursor when using one. This spares you from touching the display for interacting with on-screen elements and replicates the Mac experience. For a reliable, ergonomic mouse, go with the Logitech MX Master 4. It features a comfortable build and long battery life, making it suitable for long work hours.

If you’d rather spend less, you can buy a Microsoft-branded Bluetooth mouse for a fraction of the price. It may not offer as many customization options or perks as certain alternatives, but it’ll reliably get the job done.

External display

iPadOS is natively compatible with external monitors, letting you get work done on larger displays. M-series iPads support secondary workspaces, allowing you to simultaneously interact with different windows on the built-in screen and external one. Less powerful iPad models limit external display support to screen mirroring, which is still decent for those seeking a wider canvas.

For a dependable option, you may want to consider the Dell 27 Monitor S2725QC. It features a 4K resolution, USB-C connectivity, 120Hz refresh rate, and more. Planning to work on the go? Go with the Asus ZenScreen 15. 6 Inch Portable Monitor instead. It may not be as advanced, but it’s certainly sufficient for mobile setups.

Foundry

USB-C dongle

iPads only offer a single USB-C port, and that can limit the peripherals you can connect to them—especially during charging sessions. Fortunately, you can add more ports to your iPad by connecting a dongle. There are endless options offered by a wide range of brands, featuring various port types and price ranges that cater to all sorts of customers. Some solid dongles include those from Anker, Acer, and Ugreen. Ensure your iPad model is compatible with your selection before completing your purchase.

Docking Station

If you’re not a big fan of dangling dongles, you could opt for a docking station instead. Several excellent brands offer dedicated stands that incorporate additional ports for your iPad. They are ideal for stable setups and will maintain your desk’s minimalistic, clutter-free look. The Satechi 6-in-1 USB-C Stand Hub and Anker 551 USB-C Hub with Foldable Stand will both transform your iPad into a serious workstation.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Roblox Officially Cracks Down on Doomscrolling-Reward Games After Controversy
articles.subtitle: The Black Mirror of Roblox games just got nerfed The Roblox Corporation seems to be doing a lot of apologizing lately. After a controversial game called Steal an Egg went viral on its platform with more than 500,000 concurrent players, the company announced...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
The Black Mirror of Roblox games just got nerfed

The Roblox Corporation seems to be doing a lot of apologizing lately. After a controversial game called Steal an Egg went viral on its platform with more than 500,000 concurrent players, the company announced new restrictions this week that appear inspired by the core design of that experience. The company told Roblox developers that “games that reward ongoing media feed consumption” will no longer be allowed in Roblox Kids and Select.

“This affects games that combine media feeds, autoplay, infinite scroll, autoscroll, and rewards or implied rewards for watching,” Roblox said.

Why did Roblox make this change?

Steal an Egg broke Roblox containment earlier this week when somewhat unsettling images and videos went viral on social media. In a scene straight out of Black Mirror ’s “Fifteen Million Merits," players were seen running on in-game treadmills while seemingly forced to browse social media feeds of AI nonsense.

For context, Steal an Egg is a popular Roblox game that tasks players with raising eggs. However, there's a twist to this livestock sim: Players can skip the hard work of raising eggs by stealing them from others. Because of this threat, players are incentivized to raise their speed stat, which they can do by spending Robux (a currency purchased with real-world money) or by running on an in-game treadmill.

These treadmills are outfitted with a “feed” function that lets players doomscroll on a weird TikTok-equivalent as they make numbers go up— basically, the game combines pay-to-win monetization, idle games, and social media brain rot into a single depressing package. After backlash, Steal an Egg was briefly pulled from the Roblox store before returning without its feed feature.

A Roblox representative said the following about the guidelines update:

Roblox is built for fun and connection. As part of our ongoing commitment to providing age-appropriate experiences, we have updated our policies to help ensure games on Roblox reflect the safe, positive environment we aim to foster. We work closely with our creator community to provide clear guidance, and we regularly review and evolve our policies to stay consistent with that goal.

Just two weeks ago, the U. S. Senate opened an investigation into Roblox due to allegations of sexual abuse and exploitation of minors on the platform.

“Over the past decade, police have arrested numerous individuals for committing serious acts of violence and harm against children they met via Roblox, including grooming, sexual abuse, kidnapping, rape, and even murder,” a letter from Josh Hawley and Dick Durbin reads.

Numerous states have opened similar investigations into the platform, leading Roblox to institute ID checks and other precautionary measures against predatory behavior.

Steal an Egg was the hottest game on Roblox, and also the center of an unusual controversy

articles.title: Leaked Images Give First Look at Apple's AI Servers
articles.subtitle: Images claiming to show the inside of an Apple-made AI server, believed to power Private Cloud Compute, surfaced online this week, offering a first look at how the hardware is laid out.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Images claiming to show the inside of an Apple-made AI server, believed to power Private Cloud Compute, surfaced online this week, offering a first look at how the hardware is laid out.

The images were shared earlier this week by the X user @hsuchingpo, an account with a track record of Apple hardware and prototype leaks. Captioned simply "Apple M5 Server," the leaker said the hardware is "most likely" Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) system. Private Cloud Compute is Apple's system for offloading demanding Apple Intelligence requests from a device to the cloud while keeping user data from being stored or shared.

The images show a rack mountable chassis packed with compute modules. Each one has a separate circuit board mounted on a carrier bar and secured with blue and red ejector latches for quick removal. The boards connect into a backplane through gold edge connectors, with heatsinks running through the center of each column and a service diagram taped inside the lid mapping out numbered board positions and Apple part numbers.

苹果M5服务器 #apple pic.twitter.com/BJE4W0qPWF — 徐静环境 (@hsuchingpo) August 24, 2026

Each single chassis holds up to 32 boards. The layout appears to be built around airflow, with heatsinks running down the center and fans at both ends.

One close-up image shows a board with its thermal paste wiped away, revealing an Apple logo printed directly onto a chip package, appearing to confirm the hardware uses Apple's own silicon. Two NAND flash chips sit nearby.

The leaker added that the server cannot manage its own workload independently. In replies, they explained that the hardware "requires use in conjunction with Mac Studio (serves the function of software control)" and apart from Apple, no one can activate it, since doing so needs both a physical control machine and a control account.

Apple produces AI servers domestically at a facility in Houston, Texas, as part of a $600 billion U.S. investment commitment.

articles.title: My daughter brought a Mac to college. This is the tech I wish I’d packed for her
articles.subtitle: Macworld Going to college or university is the first long-term stay away from home for most new students. Alongside the really boring stuff—bedding, clothes hangers, notepads, and coffee cups—there’s a lot of new tech to take, and most freshmen miss...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Going to college or university is the first long-term stay away from home for most new students. Alongside the really boring stuff—bedding, clothes hangers, notepads, and coffee cups—there’s a lot of new tech to take, and most freshmen miss some of the electronic essentials that they all will need from day one in their college dorm.

You know that you’ll need a computer—most likely a portable laptop, and we recommend the best MacBook for students elsewhere. Many students—particularly those studying science subjects—find a tablet such as an Apple iPad is more convenient, and so you can read our list of the best iPads for students, too. Indeed, with the addition of a supporting keyboard, the iPad can also function as well as laptops for written assessments: see our recommendations for the best iPad keyboards.

We surveyed a bunch of second-year students and their parents to come up with this list of the essential tech and gadgets every student needs in their room and for going about their daily college life.

Charging station

The number-one forgotten electronic item when heading off to college is the humble charging station, power strip, or plug extension cord. Dorm rooms—some designed before smartphones and even laptops existed—have precious few power sockets, and the one you eventually find is sure to be located as far away as possible from where you need it. A power strip will solve nearly all a student’s room’s charging problems. Look for one with a cord of at least six feet since power outlets are always in the wrong spot.

Rather than just plugging in a standard long power strip, choose a power extender with USB ports—select one with more USB-C than older USB-A type ports, plus a handful of AC power outlets just like those on a wall socket. USB-C is the more modern connector and is required for fast charging of your iPhone, iPad and MacBook as well as many other powered items.

Baseus

U.S. students/parents should consider the Baseus EnerFill FD11 Power Strip (pictured above) that boasts six AC power outlets for larger items (kettle, printer, lamps and TV), three USB-C ports (for smartphones and tablets) and a legacy USB-A port for your older tech. Each USB-C port can handle 67W of power, which is enough power to keep a MacBook Air or a 14-inch MacBook Pro filled up.

Anker

Another option is the Anker Nano Power Strip desk clamp (above) that hosts six AC outlets, two that come up on top of the desk while the others are hidden underneath. There are two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports easily accessible above your desk too. One of the USB-C ports delivers up to 70W, which is enough to fast-charge most laptops, along with iPhones and iPads. The desk needs to be no thinner than 0.

6 inches and no thicker than 1. 8 inches, which you might not know until you get to your college room. The Baseus Power Strip is maybe less neat but more flexible.

Ugreen

U. K. parents/students should consider our previous favorite power strip, the Ugreen 100W USB-C GaN Charging Station (shown above) that is now available only in that region. It features three USB-C ports (2x 100W and 1x 22. 5W), one USB-A (22W), and three extra AC plug sockets. That should be enough for most people. If not, buy two. The 100W USB-C ports can charge even a large laptop with ease.

Ugreen has a smaller cube-shaped power extender, too: the 65W USB-C GaN Charging Station, with two USB-C (both 65W) and two USB-A (18W) ports, and three AC outlets.

Anker

Long cables

All of your Apple devices use USB-C, but you might still have some USB-A and MicroUSB devices around. Also, it’s a common misconception that all USB-C cables are basically the same, but they’re not. Some are for data transfer only. And those that do support charging vary in how fast they can charge. iPhones and tablets require around 30W of power for fast charging, while a MacBook Pro needs 60-100W.

The easiest solution is to choose a universal cable that supports up to 100W so you can use it with all your devices.

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Why A Game Originally Prototyped For Game Boy Color Is Going Head-To-Head With GTA 6
articles.subtitle: Devolver Digital Indie Indie Games Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19, and most studios have been giving its release date a wide berth for obvious reasons.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Devolver Digital Indie Indie Games

Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19, and most studios have been giving its release date a wide berth for obvious reasons. Who would want to go up against Rockstar’s giant?

Apparently, two games: a port of The Binding of Isaac, and a release from the only developer/publisher who would commit to doing such a thing as a bit: Devolver Digital.

Doinksoft, Devolver’s in-house studio, has made a Game Boy Color-style 2D platformer called Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed that it’s releasing on PC on November 19. The studio and publisher have naturally leaned into the absurdity of the release date with the game’s announcement, to the point where (given Devolver’s history) we had to check in and make sure this was, in fact, a real video game.

It is, and no, it wasn’t originally made as a marketing stunt: it’s silly, but sincere. Over email, Doinksoft designer Britt Brady and Devolver co-founder and marketing head Nigel Lowrie [the responses were attributed jointly to both] told me that Brady actually pitched the game to Devolver “well before” GTA 6 was a part of the conversation, by sending Devolver HQ a package containing an Analog Pocket and a custom Game Boy Color cartridge with a fully playable level of Volvy’s Adventure.

Though the game was prototyped for GBC and was originally planned to be released for the system just as a fun, small thing, the team agreed it deserved a bigger platform and ported it to PC, with a release on modern consoles planned for later on.

Separately, within Devolver, the team had joked about releasing a game—no specific one—on the same day as GTA 6. “As time went by and as it became clear that Volvy was destined to become a proper game, it felt inevitable that the world’s greatest gaming mascot should be the chosen one to face off with GTA 6.”

There’s a level of unintentional irony here that I can appreciate, as the embargo for their game’s news lifted right as a bunch of GTA 6 embargoes also expired, meaning the announcement of Volvy’s Adventure took place alongside several hundred GTA -related headlines.

Devolver and Doinksoft have committed, though. “There is no doubt GTA 6 will have the spotlight before, during and after November 19 but it’s not for everyone, or releasing on Steam the same day, so we figure there’s a bit of ‘counter-programming’ that may work in Volvy ’s favor.”

Volvy is, of course, the official Devolver Digital mascot, a rat-looking sort of thing with one large hand and one small hand (???) that Devolver has used as a parody of both mainstream mascot characters as well as the tendency of companies to try to “bring back” classic mascots of varying popularity. Volvy’s appeared in several Devolver-published games now, though, turning him from a parody of a mascot into an actual one, albeit one without the fame of Mario or the absurd pseudo-fame of a character like Gex.

But yes, Volvy’s Adventure is a real, retro-style 2D platformer. As Lowrie and Brady describe it: “[Volvy] is centered entirely on kinetic force, chain reactions, dynamic combos, and intense destruction. His expansive moveset naturally keeps him airborne, chaining combos that keep him from ever needing to set foot on land. Volvy boasts a large, versatile toolkit mapped to minimal, highly intuitive inputs.

The control scheme allows players to easily execute complex, momentum-based destructive sequences without ever having to fight the controls, prioritizing expression and continuous movement. ”

Apparently there are four worlds’ worth of levels, and Volvy is trying to rescue his kidnapped friends, and there’s a wizard who unleashed some slime. I’m still fuzzy on the details, but I think that’s maybe part of the goof here. The pair’s statement concluded, “If only we knew about the GTA 6 nudist colony so we could have put that in Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed too.” What can you do!

articles.content:
Switch up your look for different outfits and occasions

Express different sides of who you are

Color has never been a fixed thing. It shifts with light, with mood, with the hour of the day and the version of ourselves we bring to it. A single shade of blue can read as calm at breakfast and bold by nightfall. It’s this idea that identity is never singular—that sits at the heart of UNIQ’s new collaboration with PANTONE®: the Revix IV PANTONE® Edition Reversible Apple Watch Band.

On the surface, it’s a watch strap. Look closer, and it’s an argument about how we dress to reflect our different moods, perspectives, and sides of who we are.

UNIQ

The problem with one-sided design

Most accessories ask you to commit. One color, one texture, one mood, worn on repeat until it either becomes a signature or starts to feel stale. For a generation that moves fluidly between a client meeting, a gallery opening, and a Sunday run, that kind of rigidity feels increasingly out of step. The Revix IV starts from a different premise: that an everyday essential should flex the way a day actually does.

Its dual-color construction, finished with subtle PANTONE®-informed patterning, gives wearers up to eight distinct ways to style the band, yet in a minimalistic manner. A flip changes the entire register of the piece—from quiet and considered to unexpectedly playful—without changing the object itself. It’s the same idea PANTONE® has spent decades championing: that color is never neutral, it’s a language, and fluency in it means knowing when to switch tone.

UNIQ

Function first, always

None of this would matter if the mechanics didn’t hold up, and this is where UNIQ’s engineering does the quiet work behind the design story. A patented connector system makes the transformation between styles genuinely seamless—no tools, no fuss, just a twist and a new look. For those who want an added layer of confidence, optional matching loops reinforce the fit while doubling down on the strap’s dual-colour personality rather than hiding it.

Security, too, has been treated as non-negotiable. The upgraded magnetic attachment has been tested to withstand up to 1.3kg of pull—a reassurance for anyone who has ever felt an Apple Watch strap loosen mid-commute and wondered if their watch would survive the day. Length adjustment stays effortless, so the fit is exact rather than approximate.

Then there’s the part you feel before you see: a soft, leather-like exterior paired with a smooth, finely textured interior. It’s a small detail, but it’s the kind that separates an accessory worn out of habit from one worn with intention—comfortable enough for a twelve-hour day, refined enough not to announce itself.

UNIQ

More than a color

What makes this collaboration worth paying attention to isn’t the novelty of a reversible watch strap—plenty of brands have tried variations on that idea. It’s the thinking underneath it. UNIQ × PANTONE® isn’t simply pairing a product with a trusted color authority for credibility’s sake. It’s using color as a genuine design language, one that acknowledges that the people wearing it are not one thing, all the time.

articles.title: Hands-On with Computer History: OpenAI’s Take on Agent Memory
articles.subtitle: Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into...
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: BG3 Fans, We've Been Pronouncing Astarion's Name Wrong
articles.subtitle: A new Baldur's Gate 3: Astarion audiobook sample gave fans their first-ever chance to hear Astarion's surname spoken aloud. We're now confused
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Over the course of more than 236 hours of voice acting in Baldur’s Gate 3, no character in the game ever says Astarion’s full name out loud. We know what his last name is — the detail-loving fanbase has spent the last three years staring at “Ancunín” on Astarion’s gravestone.

But we’ve only been able to guess at how it’s meant to sound, with many of us landing somewhere around “an-KYU-nin” for an approximate pronunciation. That changed this week when a sample of the new tie-in audiobook Baldur’s Gate 3: Astarion gave us the first-ever chance to hear the name officially spoken — and by Astarion’s voice actor Neil Newbon, himself. The sound bite has taken everyone off guard.

According to the voice of Astarion, the correct pronunciation of "Ancunín" is something closer to "an-soo-neen. " The internet’s divided on whether to take this new information in stride or to, with all due respect to Newbon, say the name the way we’ve mostly agreed on since 2023.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.
